questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Where do commercial banks show the provisions held against standard assets in their balance sheet, according to RBI's IRACP Directions, 2025?

options.text: Netted from gross advances, like provisions on NPAs
Separately, as 'Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets' under 'Other Liabilities and Provisions – Others'
As part of the Interest Suspense Account
Deducted from gross NPAs to arrive at net NPAs

solution.explanation: Standard asset provisions are not netted from gross advances and are not reckoned for arriving at net NPAs; they are shown separately as 'Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets' under 'Other Liabilities and Provisions – Others' in Schedule 5 of the balance sheet.
steps: Shown in Schedule 5 as contingent provisions
solution.why_others_wrong: The Directions expressly bar netting them from gross advances or using them for net NPAs; interest suspense is a different account.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Separately, as 'Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets' under 'Other Liabilities and Provisions – Others'

fact_checks.claim: The provisions towards standard assets need not be netted from gross advances but shown separately as 'Contingent Provisions against Standard Assets' under 'Other Liabilities and Provisions Others' in Schedule 5 of the balance sheet
The provisions on standard assets shall not be reckoned for arriving at net NPAs

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's IRACP Directions, 2025, overdue receivables representing the positive mark-to-market value of a derivative contract are classified as NPA if they remain unpaid for how long from the specified due date?

solution.explanation: In respect of derivative transactions, overdue receivables representing positive mark-to-market value become NPA if they remain unpaid for 90 days from the specified due date for payment.
steps: Unpaid 90 days from due date → NPA
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 and 60 days mark SMA stages; 180 days is the limit for reviewing credit limits.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 90 days

fact_checks.claim: in respect of derivative transactions, the overdue receivables representing positive mark-to-market value of a derivative contract, remain unpaid for a period of 90 days from the specified due date for payment

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank acquires a borrower's immovable property in satisfaction of its claims (a 'specified non-financial asset', SNFA). Under RBI's Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025, the bank's policy must set a maximum period for its disposal not exceeding:

solution.explanation: An SNFA is an immovable asset acquired by a bank in full or part satisfaction of its claims, including non-banking assets. The bank's policy must cover the limit on SNFAs as a share of total assets, eligibility, delegation, recovery efforts before acquisition and a maximum disposal period not exceeding seven years.
steps: SNFA = immovable asset taken over in satisfaction of claims
solution.why_others_wrong: One, three and ten years are not the ceiling in the Directions.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Seven years

fact_checks.claim: 'specified non-financial asset' (SNFA) means an immovable asset acquired by a bank in satisfaction or part satisfaction of its claims on the borrower

Such provisions shall specify inter-alia the limit on SNFAs as a share of total assets, eligibility criteria, delegation matrix, recovery efforts to be explored before acquisition and maximum period for disposal not exceeding seven years

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under Section 31 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002, a secured creditor cannot use the Act's enforcement provisions where the amount due is less than what share of the principal amount and interest?

solution.concept: Exclusions under Section 31 of the SARFAESI Act
solution.explanation: Section 31(j) excludes cases where the amount due is less than 20% of the principal amount and interest thereon; such dues must be recovered through other routes such as the DRT. Section 31(i) separately excludes security interest created in agricultural land.
steps: Section 31 lists cases where SARFAESI does not apply
Clause (j): amount due < 20% of principal and interest
solution.why_others_wrong: 10%, 25% and 50% are not the threshold in Section 31(j).
solution.final_answer: Option A: 20 per cent

fact_checks.claim: Section 31(j): the Act does not apply where the amount due is less than twenty per cent of the principal amount and interest thereon
SARFAESI proceedings can be initiated only if the outstanding due payable by the borrower is more than 20% of principal and interest

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's IRACP Directions, 2025, a bank must normally classify assets through an automated system. If, exceptionally, a manual intervention overrides the system classification, what is required?

options.text: Approval of the statutory auditor, with logs kept for one year
At least two-level authorisation, with logs of the override stored for at least three years
Prior approval of RBI for each override
A single authorisation by the branch manager, with no logs required

solution.explanation: Manual intervention is to be avoided; where it is unavoidable it needs at least two-level authorisation under the Board-approved delegation, and logs (date and time stamp, reason, user IDs, names, designations and account details) must be stored for at least three years without tampering.
solution.why_others_wrong: Auditor approval, RBI approval per case and single authorisation without logs are not the rule.
solution.final_answer: Option B: At least two-level authorisation, with logs of the override stored for at least three years

fact_checks.claim: In any exceptional circumstance where manual intervention is required to override the System classification, it shall have at least two level authorisation
These logs shall also be stored for a minimum period of three years and not be tampered with

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: An official of an asset reconstruction company (ARC) was part of the committee that approved the acquisition of a financial asset. According to RBI's FAQs on ARCs (September 2026), what role can that official play when a settlement proposal for the same asset comes up?

options.text: None; the official cannot be part of processing or approving the settlement in any capacity
The official may approve it if the settlement is above the acquisition price
The official may process it but not approve it
The official may approve it with the Board's prior consent

solution.explanation: To segregate acquisition and settlement, any official who was part of the acquisition of a financial asset (individually or in a committee) shall not be part of either processing or approving the settlement proposal for that asset, in any capacity.
steps: Acquisition and settlement must be segregated
Acquiring official → no role in settlement
solution.why_others_wrong: No exception exists for price, a processing-only role or Board consent.
solution.final_answer: Option A: None; the official cannot be part of processing or approving the settlement in any capacity

fact_checks.claim: any official who was part of the acquisition (as an individual or part of a committee) of the concerned financial asset shall not be part of either processing or approving the proposal for settlement of the same financial asset, in any capacity

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements under RBI's IRACP Directions, 2025:
I. Specific provisions that a bank voluntarily makes on NPAs at rates higher than the regulatory minimum are treated as floating provisions.
II. Such additional provisions on NPAs may be netted off from gross NPAs to arrive at net NPAs.
III. Floating provisions cannot be reversed by credit to the profit and loss account.
IV. Amounts held in the Interest Suspense Account are reckoned as part of provisions.
Which of the above are correct?

solution.concept: Additional provisions, floating provisions and interest suspense
solution.explanation: Voluntary higher provisions on NPAs (Board-approved and consistently applied) are not floating provisions, and like the regulatory minimum they may be netted from gross NPAs. Floating provisions can only be used for specific provisions in extraordinary circumstances and are never reversed to P&L. Interest suspense balances are not provisions; they are deducted from the advance before provisioning.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing I or IV are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: II and III only

fact_checks.claim: Such additional provisions shall not be considered as floating provisions. The additional provisions for NPAs, like the minimum regulatory provision on NPAs, may be netted off from gross NPAs to arrive at the net NPAs
Floating provisions shall not be reversed by credit to the profit and loss account
Amounts held in Interest Suspense Account shall not be reckoned as part of provisions

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A domestic bank has met its overall PSL target but is short of its Micro Enterprises sub-target. Under RBI's PSLC guidelines in the PSL Directions, 2025, which certificate must it buy to cover this shortfall?

solution.concept: Matching PSLC type to the shortfall

A bank short of a specific sub-target must buy the specific PSLC; PSLC – General counts only towards the overall target, and the agriculture and SF/MF certificates count towards farm targets.
steps: Buy the specific PSLC → PSLC – Micro Enterprises
solution.why_others_wrong: PSLC – General counts only for the overall target; agriculture and SF/MF certificates do not count for micro enterprises.
solution.final_answer: Option D: PSLC – Micro Enterprises

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank has purchased bills drawn under a letter of credit (payment to the beneficiary not under reserve). For computing 'bank credit in India' and ANBC for PSL, what do RBI's PSL FAQs say?

options.text: They must not be excluded from bank credit in India; if the advance is PSL-eligible it can be classified as PSL
They are excluded as inter-bank exposure, since the LC-issuing bank bears the risk
They are excluded from bank credit but may still be counted as PSL achievement
They count only if the LC-issuing bank is a scheduled commercial bank

solution.explanation: Such bills may be treated as inter-bank exposure only for computing exposure and capital requirements. They amount to bank credit to the borrower and must not be excluded from 'bank credit in India'; if the advance is eligible, the bank can classify it as PSL.
steps: Remains in bank credit in India / ANBC
solution.why_others_wrong: Exclusion from bank credit is not allowed; there is no condition about the type of LC-issuing bank.
solution.final_answer: Option A: They must not be excluded from bank credit in India; if the advance is PSL-eligible it can be classified as PSL

fact_checks.claim: The bills purchased/ discounted/ negotiated (payment to beneficiary not under reserve) under LC is allowed to be treated as interbank exposure only for the limited purpose of computing exposure and capital requirements. It should not be excluded from the computation of 'bank credit in India' ... If this advance is eligible for priority sector classification, the bank can classify it as PSL

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under a co-lending arrangement between a bank and an NBFC for priority sector loans, RBI's PSL FAQs explain what 'back-to-back basis' means. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bank first opens the loan accounts, and the NBFC follows
Both open and fund their loan accounts simultaneously on a single date
The NBFC first opens the loan accounts, and the bank opens its share of the loan accounts subsequently
The NBFC retains 100% of the risk on the bank's share

solution.explanation: RBI clarified that back-to-back basis implies the loans are first opened by the NBFC and then the bank opens its loan accounts. It also said that PSL assets on the bank's books must at all times be without recourse to the NBFC.
steps: Bank's PSL assets: no recourse to NBFC
solution.why_others_wrong: The order is NBFC first; simultaneous opening is not what back-to-back means; the NBFC cannot carry the bank's risk, as the bank's PSL assets must be without recourse.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The NBFC first opens the loan accounts, and the bank opens its share of the loan accounts subsequently

fact_checks.claim: Back-to-back basis implies that the loans will be first opened by NBFC and then bank will open loan accounts subsequently
the priority sector assets on the bank's books should at all times be without recourse to the NBFC

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Bank D (domestic, ANBC ₹1,50,000 crore) has incremental export credit of ₹3,200 crore over the corresponding date of the previous year, of which ₹600 crore is to borrowers with sanctioned limits above ₹50 crore. Bank F (a foreign bank with 25 branches, ANBC ₹50,000 crore) has incremental export credit of ₹900 crore, of which ₹300 crore is to borrowers with sanctioned limits above ₹50 crore. ANBC is higher than CEOBSE for both, and none of this credit is to agriculture or MSMEs. How much export credit can each classify as priority sector?

solution.explanation: Domestic banks may count incremental export credit up to 2% of ANBC, with a sanctioned limit of up to ₹50 crore per borrower: (3,200 − 600) = 2,600, below 2% × 1,50,000 = 3,000, so ₹2,600 crore. Foreign banks with 20 or more branches may count incremental export credit up to 2% of ANBC without the per-borrower cap: 900, below 2% × 50,000 = 1,000, so ₹900 crore.
steps: D: exclude large-sanction borrowers → 2,600; cap 3,000 → ₹2,600 crore
F: no per-borrower cap → 900; cap 1,000 → ₹900 crore
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹3,000 crore for D ignores the ₹50 crore sanction limit; ₹600 crore for F wrongly applies that limit to a foreign bank with 20+ branches.
solution.final_answer: Option B: D: ₹2,600 crore; F: ₹900 crore

fact_checks.claim: Domestic banks/WoS of Foreign banks/SFBs/UCBs: Incremental export credit over corresponding date of the preceding year, up to 2 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE whichever is higher, subject to a sanctioned limit of up to ₹50 crore per borrower. Foreign banks with 20 branches and above: Incremental export credit over corresponding date of the preceding year, up to 2 percent of ANBC or CEOBSE whichever is higher

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A domestic bank's ANBC (higher than CEOBSE) is ₹10,000 crore for all four quarters of a year, and its PSL target is 40%. Its own priority sector lending equals 37%, 38%, 38% and 39% of ANBC on the four quarterly reporting dates (30 June, 30 September, 31 December, 31 March). On 15 July it buys a PSLC – General of ₹100 crore. Following RBI's illustration on when a purchased PSLC is reckoned, and RBI's method for the annual shortfall, what is the bank's shortfall for the year?

solution.concept: Timing of PSLC reckoning and the annual shortfall
solution.explanation: A PSLC bought on 15 July is reckoned on the reporting dates of 30 September, 31 December and 31 March (not 30 June). ₹100 crore is 1% of ANBC, so achievements become 37, 39, 39 and 40%; quarterly shortfalls are 3, 1, 1 and 0. The year's shortfall is their simple average: 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25 percentage points.
steps: PSLC (1 pp) counts in Q2, Q3, Q4 only
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.00 ignores the PSLC; 1.00 counts it in the June quarter too; 0.25 takes only the last quarter's position.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1.25 percentage points

fact_checks.claim: Bank A may sell PSLCs with a nominal value of ₹100 crores to Bank B on July 15, 2025. Bank B will reckon ₹100 crore towards its priority sector achievement as on the reporting dates of September 30, 2025, December 31, 2025 & March 31, 2026
The shortfall/ excess for the year is arrived at by taking a simple average of the shortfall/excess for all the four quarters

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: As a consumer protection measure under RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025, how should a Business Correspondent's retail outlet or sub-agent be introduced to the public?

options.text: Through an advertisement issued by the BC company
By an RBI notification listing all BC outlets
By the Gram Panchayat alone, without bank officials

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following must a bank's arrangement with a Business Correspondent specify, under RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025?

options.text: Suitable limits on cash holding by the BC and on individual customer payments and receipts
That the BC may introduce its own products once it informs the bank
That financial services at the outlet may be tied to the sale of the BC company's products
That the BC may charge customers a fee directly for services rendered for the bank

solution.explanation: Arrangements must specify limits on cash holding and on individual customer payments and receipts, issue of receipts on the bank's behalf, end-of-day accounting of off-line transactions and the bank's responsibility for the BC's acts. BCs cannot introduce products without the bank's approval, cannot tie services to their own products and cannot charge customers directly.
steps: Prohibited: own products, tie-ins, direct fees
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are expressly prohibited.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Suitable limits on cash holding by the BC and on individual customer payments and receipts

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to SBI's FAQs on PMJDY (describing RBI's BSBD guidelines), how many free withdrawals, including ATM transactions, must a BSBD account get every month at a minimum, and how are UPI, NEFT or IMPS payments treated?

options.text: At least four; every UPI, NEFT or IMPS payment counts as one withdrawal
At least five; digital payments count as half a withdrawal
At least four; digital payments such as UPI, NEFT and IMPS are not counted as withdrawals
Unlimited withdrawals at own-bank ATMs only

solution.explanation: A BSBD account gets a minimum of four free withdrawals and ATM transactions (own or other banks' ATMs) a month. Digital payments other than ATM transactions — PoS, NEFT, RTGS, UPI, IMPS and so on — are not counted as withdrawals for this purpose.
steps: Minimum four free withdrawals/ATM transactions a month
Digital payments excluded from the count
solution.why_others_wrong: Digital payments are not counted; five, half-counting and own-ATM-only are not the rule.
solution.final_answer: Option C: At least four; digital payments such as UPI, NEFT and IMPS are not counted as withdrawals

Digital payment transactions excluding ATM transactions, i.e., Point of Sale transfers, NEFT, RTGS, UPI, IMPS, etc., shall not be counted as withdrawals for this purpose

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: How should transactions put through Business Correspondents normally be processed, under RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025?

options.text: In a paper register at the BC outlet, posted to CBS weekly
Through the BC company's own ledger, settled with the bank monthly
Only at the base Banking Outlet, with the BC collecting forms
Through ICT devices integrated with the bank's CBS, accounted for in real time, with immediate verification to the customer

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Three PMJDY account holders with RuPay debit cards die in accidents. P opened her account in March 2017 and last used her card 40 days before the accident. Q opened his account in January 2020; his last transaction on any channel was 120 days before the accident. R opened his account in 2022 and made a balance enquiry at a CSP 10 days before the accident. Based on the Government's PM-JDY note and SBI's PMJDY FAQs, what accident insurance is payable?

options.text: P ₹1 lakh; Q nil; R ₹2 lakh
P ₹2 lakh; Q ₹2 lakh; R ₹2 lakh
P ₹1 lakh; Q ₹2 lakh; R ₹2 lakh
P ₹1 lakh; Q nil; R nil

solution.concept: Conditions for the RuPay card accident cover
solution.explanation: The cover is ₹1 lakh, enhanced to ₹2 lakh for new PMJDY accounts opened after August 2018. It is payable only if the cardholder made at least one successful financial or non-financial transaction on any channel within 90 days before the accident (including the accident date). P: old account, active → ₹1 lakh. Q: no transaction in 90 days → nil. R: new account; a balance enquiry is a non-financial transaction → ₹2 lakh.
steps: P: opened before Aug 2018, active → ₹1 lakh
R: opened after Aug 2018, non-financial transaction counts → ₹2 lakh
solution.why_others_wrong: Q fails the 90-day activity test; P's account predates the enhancement; R's balance enquiry counts.
solution.final_answer: Option A: P ₹1 lakh; Q nil; R ₹2 lakh

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about consumer protection in the Business Correspondent model under RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025:
I. A BC may introduce a new product at its outlets without the bank's approval if it informs the base Banking Outlet.
II. The charges for various services must be indicated in a brochure available at the retail outlets or with the sub-agents.
III. The bank must have a business continuity plan to ensure uninterrupted service if the agency arrangement with the BC is terminated.
Which of the above are correct?

Charges must be shown in a brochure at the outlets, and the bank must have a business continuity plan for uninterrupted service if the BC arrangement ends.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing I are wrong.

II: KVKs are in the BF list only → wrong

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about remuneration and oversight of Business Correspondents under RBI's Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025:
I. The commission structure must be designed so that a mere increase in the number of clients or transaction volume does not drive the commission.
II. The Board (or its delegated committee) must review the operations of BCs at least once every six months, with a view to tapering down pre-funding by BCs.
III. Pre-funding should ideally come down, within two years of a BC starting operations, to around 30% of the limits for deposits and 15% for bank guarantees.
Which of the above are correct?

solution.explanation: Commission must not be driven merely by the number of clients or transactions; remuneration combines fixed and variable parts linked to customer satisfaction. The Board or its committee reviews BC operations at least every six months so that pre-funding tapers down, ideally to around 15% of the limits for deposits and 30% for bank guarantees within two years. Statement III swaps these figures.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing III are wrong because the percentages are reversed.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Commission structure or incentive mechanism shall be devised in a manner that mere increase in the number of clients served or the transaction volume does not drive the commission

The Board or any committee ... shall review the operations of BCs at least once every six months with a view to ensuring that requirement of prefunding ... should progressively taper down ... so as to reach around 15 percent of the limits fixed for each BC / CSP in case of deposits and 30 percent in case of Bank Guarantees, etc. in two years

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: During a period of financial stress, a bank uses part of its stock of HQLA and its LCR falls below 100 per cent. What does RBI's LCR framework require it to do?

options.text: Nothing, as the LCR is only a monitoring tool
Stop all lending until the LCR is restored
Immediately report the shortfall to RBI's Department of Supervision, with reasons and corrective steps
Pay a penal rate of interest on the shortfall to RBI for every day of the shortfall

solution.explanation: The LCR must normally be at least 100%, but in stress a bank may use its HQLA and let the ratio fall below 100%. It must then immediately report the shortfall to the Department of Supervision, RBI, with the reasons and the corrective steps initiated.
steps: LCR < 100% → immediate report to DoS with reasons and remedial steps
solution.why_others_wrong: The LCR is a binding minimum; RBI does not require a lending freeze or a daily penal charge for this.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Immediately report the shortfall to RBI's Department of Supervision, with reasons and corrective steps

fact_checks.claim: during a period of financial stress, a bank shall have the option to use its stock of HQLA and thereby allowing LCR to fall below 100 per cent. In such a case, the bank shall immediately report the shortfall to DoS, RBI. The report shall include reasons for such usage and corrective steps initiated

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: At what level does RBI's LCR framework apply to a foreign bank operating in India through branches?

options.text: On a consolidated basis for the global group
Only to its largest branch in India
It does not apply to foreign bank branches
On a standalone basis, for its Indian operations only

solution.explanation: The LCR applies to an Indian bank on a solo and a consolidated basis. For a foreign bank operating as branches in India it applies on a standalone basis, i.e. to its Indian operations only.
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI does not apply its LCR to the foreign bank's global group, to one branch only, or exempt the branches.
solution.final_answer: Option D: On a standalone basis, for its Indian operations only

fact_checks.claim: The LCR framework shall be applicable to an Indian bank on a standalone ('solo') as well as consolidated level. For a foreign bank operating as branch in India, the framework shall be applicable on standalone basis i.e., for Indian operations only

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: The Basel Committee's post-crisis Basel III reforms were endorsed in December 2017 by its oversight body. What is that body?

options.text: The Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS)
The International Monetary and Financial Committee of the IMF

solution.explanation: The BIS notes that the post-crisis regulatory reforms were endorsed on 7 December 2017 by the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS), the Basel Committee's oversight body.
solution.why_others_wrong: The G20, FATF and IMFC are not the Basel Committee's oversight body.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS)

fact_checks.claim: The post-crisis regulatory reforms were endorsed by the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS), the Basel Committee's oversight body, on 7 December 2017

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: RBI's liquidity risk management directions draw on a Basel Committee document published after the global financial crisis. Which document, published in September 2008, is it?

options.text: Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision
Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision
International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards

solution.explanation: RBI notes that, after the crisis, the BCBS published 'Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision' in September 2008, later reviewed in January 2019; its broad principles are reproduced in the Asset Liability Management Directions.
steps: September 2008 → Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision
solution.why_others_wrong: The Core Principles (1997), the 1988 Capital Accord and market-risk standards are different documents.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision

fact_checks.claim: the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) published 'Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision' in September 2008 and subsequently reviewed in January 2019

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements on Required Stable Funding (RSF) factors under RBI's NSFR rules:
I. Unencumbered SLR securities attract an RSF factor of 5%.
II. Physically traded commodities, including gold, attract an RSF factor of 85%.
III. Loans to financial institutions with a residual maturity of one year or more attract an RSF factor of 65%.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: Unencumbered Level 1 assets and SLR securities get 5%; physical traded commodities including gold get 85%; loans to financial institutions with residual maturity of one year or more fall in the 100% category (the 65% factor is for other unencumbered loans of a year or more, excluding loans to financial institutions, such as loans to sovereigns and NDBs).
steps: III: FI loans ≥ 1 year → 100%, not 65% – wrong
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement III is false, so options including it are wrong; 'II only' misses the true statement I.
solution.final_answer: Option B: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: Assets assigned a 5 per cent RSF factor comprise (1) Unencumbered Level 1 assets ... (2) Unencumbered SLR securities; 85 per cent RSF factor: (7) Physical traded commodities, including gold

100 per cent RSF factor: All other assets not included in the above categories, including non-performing loans, loans to financial institutions with a residual maturity of one year or more, non-exchange traded equities, fixed assets

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Over the next 30 days a bank has these maturing secured loans: a reverse repo of ₹200 crore secured by Level 1 assets, a reverse repo of ₹100 crore secured by non-HQLA assets, and margin loans of ₹80 crore to customers against non-HQLA collateral. Under RBI's LCR rules, what total cash inflow can it recognise from these?

solution.concept: Inflows from secured lending in the LCR
solution.explanation: Maturing reverse repos secured by Level 1 assets are assumed to roll over, so 0% inflow. Those secured by non-HQLA are assumed not to roll over, so 100% (₹100 crore). For margin loans against non-HQLA collateral, no more than 50% of contractual inflows can be recognised (₹40 crore). Total = ₹140 crore.
solution.why_others_wrong: ₹380 crore counts everything at 100%; ₹180 crore takes the margin loans at 100%; ₹100 crore ignores the margin loans.
solution.final_answer: Option D: ₹140 crore

fact_checks.claim: A bank shall assume that maturing reverse repurchase or securities borrowing agreements secured by Level 1 assets will be rolled over, and therefore will not give rise to any cash inflows, i.e., zero per cent cash inflow ... A bank is assumed not to roll-over maturing reverse repurchase or securities borrowing agreements secured by non-HQLA assets and can assume to receive back 100 per cent of the cash
a bank shall recognise no more than 50 per cent of contractual inflows from maturing margin loans made against non-HQLA collateral

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements on Basel III, based on the Bank for International Settlements' account:
I. The Basel Committee issued the full text of the revised Liquidity Coverage Ratio after its endorsement by the GHOS on 6 January 2013.
II. The first Basel III text was published in December 2012 and has not been updated since.
III. The Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP), which monitors implementation of Basel standards, was established in 2012.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: The revised LCR text followed GHOS endorsement on 6 January 2013. The initial Basel III document was published in December 2010 and updated in June 2011, so statement II is wrong. The RCAP was set up in 2012 to monitor timely and consistent adoption of Basel III.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with II are wrong; 'I only' leaves out the correct statement III.
solution.final_answer: Option C: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: The Basel Committee issued the full text of the revised Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) following endorsement on 6 January 2013 by its governing body - the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision (GHOS); This document, originally published in December 2010 and updated in June 2011 represents the initial phase of Basel III reforms
The Basel Committee established a comprehensive Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) in 2012 to monitor and assess the adoption and implementation of its standards

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: After registering a complaint with the RBI Ombudsman, how can a complainant track its status on RBI's CMS portal?

options.text: Using the bank account number and IFSC
Using the Aadhaar number and PAN
Only by visiting the Office of the RBI Ombudsman
Using the complaint number and mobile number

solution.explanation: On successful registration the complainant gets a complaint number; the status can be tracked on the CMS portal with the complaint number and mobile number, or through the Contact Centre (14448).
steps: Complaint number + mobile number → status on CMS
solution.why_others_wrong: Account/IFSC and Aadhaar/PAN are not used; no office visit is needed.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Using the complaint number and mobile number

fact_checks.claim: The status of the complaint can be tracked through the CMS portal using the complaint number and mobile number

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Annual Report of the Ombudsman Scheme 2024-25, about how many complaints were received under the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme in 2024-25?

solution.explanation: 13,34,244 complaints were received in 2024-25 against 11,75,075 in 2023-24, a rise of 13.55%. Of the total, 9.11 lakh came to the CRPC and 2.96 lakh to the Offices of RBI Ombudsman.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11.75 lakh is the 2023-24 figure; 9.11 lakh and 2.96 lakh are the CRPC and ORBIO parts.
solution.final_answer: Option B: 13.34 lakh

fact_checks.claim: Under the RB-IOS, 13,34,244 complaints were received in F.Y.2024-25 as compared to 11,75,075 in F.Y.2023-24, an increase of 13.55 per cent over the previous year

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Annual Report of the Ombudsman Scheme 2024-25, from which population group did the largest share of complaints received at the Offices of RBI Ombudsman come?

solution.explanation: In 2024-25, 45.86% of complaints came from metropolitan centres, followed by urban (25.64%), semi-urban (18.46%) and rural areas (10.04%).
solution.why_others_wrong: Urban, semi-urban and rural areas each had smaller shares.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Metropolitan centres

fact_checks.claim: majority of complaints at the ORBIOs were received from Metropolitan Centres (45.86 per cent), followed by Urban (25.64 per cent), Semi Urban (18.46 per cent) and Rural areas (10.04 per cent)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Annual Report of the Ombudsman Scheme 2024-25, which statement about complaints against banks received at the Offices of RBI Ombudsman is correct?

options.text: Private sector banks had the highest share among banks (37.53%), overtaking public sector banks (34.80%)
Public sector banks continued to have the highest share among banks, at over 38%
Small finance banks had the highest share among banks
Complaints against NBFCs outnumbered those against banks

solution.explanation: Banks accounted for 81.53% of complaints (NBFCs 14.80%). Among banks, the share of private sector banks rose from 34.39% to 37.53%, while that of public sector banks, the highest in 2023-24, fell from 38.32% to 34.80%.
solution.why_others_wrong: PSBs were highest only in 2023-24; SFBs were not the highest; NBFCs were far fewer than banks.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Private sector banks had the highest share among banks (37.53%), overtaking public sector banks (34.80%)

fact_checks.claim: Among the banks, the share of complaints received against private sector banks was the highest and increased from 34.39 per cent in F.Y.2023-24 to 37.53 per cent in F.Y.2024-25. However, the share of complaints received against the public sector banks, which was the highest in F.Y.2023-24, declined from 38.32 per cent in F.Y. 2023-24 to 34.80 per cent in F.Y.2024-25

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following banks is covered by RB-IOS, 2026?

options.text: A non-scheduled primary (urban) co-operative bank with deposits of ₹30 crore

solution.explanation: RB-IOS, 2026 covers all commercial banks, RRBs, State Co-operative Banks, Central Co-operative Banks, scheduled UCBs and non-scheduled UCBs with deposits of ₹50 crore and above. HFCs and CICs are among the excluded NBFC types.
solution.why_others_wrong: The UCB is below the ₹50 crore threshold; HFCs and CICs are expressly excluded.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A District Central Co-operative Bank

fact_checks.claim: Banks: all Commercial Banks, Regional Rural Banks, State Co-operative Banks, Central Co-operative Banks, Scheduled Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks, and Non-Scheduled Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks with deposit size of Rs 50 crore and above
NBFCs: all NBFCs registered with RBI, excluding Housing Finance Companies, Core Investment Companies

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: In RBI's Annual Report of the Ombudsman Scheme 2024-25, the largest group of non-maintainable complaints closed by the Offices of RBI Ombudsman were 'First Resort Complaints'. What are these?

options.text: Complaints filed for the first time by a customer under any ombudsman scheme
Complaints filed with the RBI Ombudsman without the complainant first approaching the regulated entity
Complaints filed within the first 30 days of opening an account
Complaints first filed in a civil court

solution.explanation: FRCs are complaints received at the ORBIOs without the complainant having approached the concerned RE first. They are sent to the RE for redress, and the complainant is told he may complain again if the RE does not reply within 30 days or the reply is unsatisfactory. They formed 33.01% of the non-maintainable complaints closed by ORBIOs in 2024-25.
steps: No prior complaint to the RE → First Resort Complaint → sent to the RE
solution.why_others_wrong: The term has nothing to do with first-time complainants, new accounts or court cases.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Complaints filed with the RBI Ombudsman without the complainant first approaching the regulated entity

fact_checks.claim: Of these, 33.01 per cent (36,289 complaints) were closed as First Resort Complaints (FRCs) ... FRCs are those complaints which are received at the ORBIOs without the complainant having approached the concerned RE first

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre (CRPC) in 2024-25, as reported in RBI's Annual Report of the Ombudsman Scheme 2024-25:
I. Complaints received at the CRPC grew much faster (18.83%) than those received at the Offices of RBI Ombudsman (0.82%).
II. Most complaints disposed of at the CRPC were assigned to the Offices of RBI Ombudsman for examination.
III. E-mail was the channel for 93.18% of the complaints received at the CRPC.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: CRPC complaints rose 18.83% (7,66,957 to 9,11,384) while ORBIO complaints rose 0.82%. Of 9.04 lakh complaints disposed at the CRPC, only 1.20 lakh were assigned to ORBIOs/CEPCs; 7.84 lakh were closed at the CRPC as non-complaints or non-maintainable, mostly First Resort Complaints. 93.18% of CRPC complaints came by e-mail.
steps: II: wrong – 1.20 lakh of 9.04 lakh assigned
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false, which rules out the options containing it; 'III only' omits the correct statement I.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I and III only

fact_checks.claim: The complaints received at the CRPC increased by 18.83 per cent from 7,66,957 complaints in F.Y.2023-24 to 9,11,384 complaints in F.Y.2024-25, while those received at the ORBIOs ... increased by 0.82 per cent

the CRPC has received 9.11 lakh complaints and disposed 9.04 lakh complaints ... Out of these, 1.20 lakh complaints were assigned to ORBIOs/CEPCs, while the remaining 7.84 lakh complaints were closed at the CRPC as non-complaint / non-maintainable complaints
During F.Y.2024-25, 93.18 per cent of the complaints received at the CRPC were through email

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Under RBI's Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026, what must a bank do about fake or malicious apps with names or features similar to its own mobile banking app?

options.text: Nothing, as app stores alone are responsible
Report them only in its annual report
Ask customers to verify apps by visiting a branch
Actively monitor popular app stores and the web for them and respond to get them taken down

solution.explanation: Banks must institute a mechanism to actively monitor popular app stores and the web for non-genuine, unauthorised or malicious applications with similar names or features, and respond appropriately to bring them down. They must also publish the checksum of their genuine app.
steps: Monitor app stores and the web → act to take down rogue apps
solution.why_others_wrong: The duty lies with the bank and calls for active monitoring and takedown, not passive reporting.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Actively monitor popular app stores and the web for them and respond to get them taken down

fact_checks.claim: The bank shall institute a mechanism to actively monitor for non-genuine / unauthorised / malicious applications (with similar name / features) on popular app-stores and the web and respond appropriately to bring them down

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: By what date did RBI require all payment system providers and participants to comply with its Authentication mechanisms for digital payment transactions Directions, 2025 (unless a provision specified otherwise)?

solution.explanation: The Directions, dated 25 September 2025 and issued under the PSS Act, 2007, required all payment system providers and participants, banks and non-banks, to comply by 1 April 2026. A separate deadline of 1 October 2026 applied to cross-border card-not-present validation.
solution.why_others_wrong: 25 September 2025 is the date of issue; 1 October 2026 is the cross-border CNP deadline; 1 January 2026 is not the date.
solution.final_answer: Option C: 1 April 2026

fact_checks.claim: All Payment System Providers and Payment System Participants, including banks and non-bank entities, shall ensure compliance with these directions by April 01, 2026, unless indicated otherwise for any specific provision herein

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: An entity wishes to test a CBDC-related use case in RBI's CBDC and Asset Tokenisation (CAT) Sandbox. To which department of RBI should it send its request?

options.text: Department of Payment and Settlement Systems

solution.why_others_wrong: The other departments do not handle CAT Sandbox access.
solution.final_answer: Option B: FinTech Department

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A customer pays an online merchant through a payment aggregator. Under RBI's Digital Payment Security Controls Directions, 2026, whose name should the bank's alert and OTP for this transaction show?

solution.explanation: Alerts and OTPs received by the customer for online transactions shall identify the merchant name, wherever applicable, rather than the payment aggregator through which the transaction was effected, so that the customer can recognise the payment.
steps: Alert/OTP → merchant name, not the aggregator
solution.why_others_wrong: Showing the aggregator, network or only the bank defeats the purpose of identifying the payee.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The merchant's name, wherever applicable

fact_checks.claim: The alerts and OTPs received by the customer for online transactions shall identify the merchant name, wherever applicable, rather than the payment aggregator through which the transaction was effected

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about customer conduct rules in RBI's Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025:
I. Banks must obtain the customer's explicit consent, duly recorded, for registering or de-registering for digital banking services.
II. Terms and conditions for registration should be in clear and simple language, preferably in English, Hindi and the local language.
III. Banks may obtain and record the mobile numbers of all customers to send transaction and other alerts.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: All three reproduce the Directions: explicit, recorded consent for registration (para 10.1); terms in clear, simple language, preferably English, Hindi and the local language (para 10.3); and, although no digital channel may be made compulsory for other facilities, banks can obtain and record mobile numbers of all customers to send alerts (para 10.5).
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other options leaves out at least one correct statement.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I, II and III

fact_checks.claim: Banks shall obtain explicit consent from the customer for registering/de-registering (in case of existing customers) for digital banking services and the consent shall be duly recorded/documented; For registration, banks shall provide the terms and conditions in clear and simple language (preferably in English, Hindi, and the local language)
The banks can, however, obtain and record mobile numbers of all customers to send transaction or other alerts

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A remitter wants to send money to Nepal through NEFT under the Indo-Nepal Remittance Facility. If the remitter holds an account with an NEFT-enabled bank branch in India, what additional identification documents must be submitted?

options.text: Passport and visa of the remitter
PAN card and a letter from the employer
None; no additional information, documents or identification is needed
Proof of the beneficiary's account with a Nepalese bank

solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs say a remitter who maintains an account with a bank branch in India need not give any additional information, documents or identification. A walk-in remitter must submit proof of identity such as passport, PAN, driving licence, telephone bill or employer's certificate.
solution.why_others_wrong: Identity documents are needed only from walk-in customers; the beneficiary need not hold a bank account.
solution.final_answer: Option C: None; no additional information, documents or identification is needed

fact_checks.claim: If the remitting customer maintains an account with a bank branch in India, there is no need for any additional information, documents or identification. Else, the remitter has to submit documents for proof of identification

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A bank in India and a bank in Nepal enter into their own bilateral arrangement to handle remittances between the two countries. According to RBI's FAQs, is this arrangement covered by the Indo-Nepal Remittance Facility Scheme?

options.text: No; INRF exclusively uses the NEFT ecosystem, and bilateral arrangements are outside its guidelines
Yes; all India–Nepal remittances by banks fall under INRF
Yes, if the Indian bank is a public sector bank
Only if the Nepalese bank is a subsidiary of an Indian bank

solution.explanation: RBI's FAQs say bilateral arrangements between banks or non-banks to handle India–Nepal cross-border transactions are not covered by the INRF guidelines; the scheme exclusively uses the NEFT ecosystem, and all NEFT-enabled branches are already covered.
solution.why_others_wrong: RBI states plainly that bilateral arrangements are not covered, irrespective of the banks' ownership.
solution.final_answer: Option A: No; INRF exclusively uses the NEFT ecosystem, and bilateral arrangements are outside its guidelines

fact_checks.claim: No. The bilateral arrangements between banks / non-banks to handle cross-border transactions between India and Nepal are not covered under guidelines of the INRF Scheme. The INRF Scheme exclusively uses NEFT ecosystem for such remittance to Nepal

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A walk-in customer paid cash at an Indian bank branch to send money to Nepal under INRF, but the money could not be delivered and has flowed back through NEFT. According to RBI's FAQs, how does the customer get the refund?

options.text: It is automatically credited to any bank account the customer names later
By producing evidence of the remittance, the counterfoil of the remittance application form
By applying to Nepal SBI Ltd, which refunds in Nepalese rupees
By filing a claim with RBI's NEFT Help Desk

solution.explanation: Undelivered amounts flow back through NEFT to the originating branch. If the remittance was made by debit to an account, the amount is credited back to that account; a walk-in remitter who paid cash must produce proof of remittance, the counterfoil of the application form, to get the refund.
steps: Account remitter → credited back to account
Walk-in cash remitter → refund against counterfoil
solution.why_others_wrong: There is no automatic credit to a new account, no refund in Nepal and no claim with RBI.
solution.final_answer: Option B: By producing evidence of the remittance, the counterfoil of the remittance application form

fact_checks.claim: If the remittance was made by a walk-in customer through a cash deposit, the remitter has to produce evidence of proof of remittance (counterfoil of the remittance application form) for getting refund

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text:
Consider the following statements about the Indo-Nepal Remittance Facility (INRF) Scheme, based on RBI's FAQs:
I. A sender who maintains an account with an NEFT-enabled branch faces no limit on the number of remittances in a year.
II. Of the ₹20 charged by SBI per remittance (up to ₹50,000), ₹10 is shared with Nepal SBI Ltd.
III. Nepal SBI Ltd charges an additional amount for crediting a beneficiary who holds an account with it.
Which of the above is/are correct?

solution.explanation: Account-holding senders face no limit on the number of remittances (walk-in customers are limited to 12 a year) — I is correct. SBI's ₹20 is shared with NSBL at ₹10 each — II is correct. NSBL does not charge anything extra for crediting a beneficiary who has an account with it; the extra ₹50/₹75 applies only when the beneficiary has no NSBL account — III is wrong.
steps: III → wrong (extra only without NSBL account)
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with III are wrong; 'II only' wrongly rejects I.
solution.final_answer: Option D: I and II only

fact_checks.claim: There is no limit on remittances if the sender is maintaining account with any NEFT enabled bank-branch in India

State Bank of India – ₹20/- per transaction. SBI would share this ₹20/- with NSBL at ₹10 each. NSBL would not charge any additional amount for crediting the beneficiary. if he maintains an account with it

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: Which of the following is listed in RBI's RTGS FAQs as a benefit of using RTGS?

options.text: RBI guarantees a minimum interest on the amount in transit
Transfers can be scheduled for any future date
There is no need to give the beneficiary's account number

solution.explanation: RBI lists RTGS benefits such as safety, no amount cap set by RBI, 24x7x365 availability, real-time transfer, no need for physical cheques or drafts, capped charges and legal backing for the transaction.
steps: Benefits include: legal backing, capped charges, 24x7, real-time credit
solution.why_others_wrong: No interest is paid on transit funds; RTGS does not accept future value-dated transactions; the beneficiary account number is essential.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The transaction has legal backing

fact_checks.claim: The transaction charges have been capped by RBI. The transaction has legal backing

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: According to RBI's Payment Systems Report (December 2025), India's large value payment systems (LVPS) consist of RBI's RTGS and the systems operated by:

options.text: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)
The Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL)

solution.explanation: RBI describes LVPS (wholesale payment systems) as those for large-value, high-priority payments such as money market, securities and interbank settlements. In India they include RBI-operated RTGS and CCIL-operated systems: Government securities clearing, forex clearing and rupee derivatives.
steps: LVPS = RTGS (RBI) + CCIL systems (G-sec, forex, rupee derivatives)
solution.why_others_wrong: NPCI and NBBL run retail systems; IBA does not operate payment systems.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL)

fact_checks.claim: In India, LVPS include RBI-operated system viz. Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) and systems operated by Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL)

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness
questions.question_text: A businessman wants his bank to pull ₹10 lakh through RTGS from a customer's account in another bank, which owes him money. According to RBI's FAQs, can such a transaction be originated?

options.text: No; RTGS is a credit-push system and only the payer can originate a transfer to the beneficiary
Yes, if the amount is ₹2 lakh or more
Yes, but only on working days during business hours
Yes, if the debtor's bank gives positive confirmation

questions.subject: Banking and Financial Awareness

Using these figures over the four years, which compound annual growth rates (CAGR) are closest?

options.text: Volume about 19% a year; value about 4.5% a year
Volume about 4.8% a year; value about 24.3% a year
Volume about 1.1% a year; value about 4.6% a year
Volume about 4.5% a year; value about 18.5% a year

solution.explanation: CAGR = (end ÷ start)^(1/years) − 1 over 4 years. Volume: (518 ÷ 434)^0.25 − 1 ≈ 4.5%. Value: (75 ÷ 38)^0.25 − 1 ≈ 18.5%; RBI, using unrounded data, reports 4.5% and 18.1%. Slow volume growth with fast value growth means IMPS is used for larger transfers.
solution.why_others_wrong: The second option swaps the two; 4.8% and 24.3% are simple averages (total growth ÷ 4); 1.1% and 4.6% divide the CAGR by four again.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Volume about 4.5% a year; value about 18.5% a year
